lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you used a chart in a talk. What should you say as you show it? (What it shows, while pointing to it.) Today: present your findings clearly, with media that earn their place.
Plan first. Sum up your findings in one sentence. Choose two or three salient points, the most important ones, and give each its evidence. Cut anything that does not support them.

Media earn their place when they make a point clearer, strengthen your evidence or add interest: a chart for numbers, a photo or a short clip to show something, a map for places, a recording to hear. Never use media just to decorate.
A clear slide has one idea, a short title, a few key words in big text, and one strong chart or picture. Keep your script in your speaker notes, not on the slide.
A busy slide fails: walls of tiny text, clashing colours and spinning effects make the audience read instead of listen. Cut it back to the key words, and say the rest.

picture.title: Plastic on our beach
bullets: Some of it is very small
Nets and ropes last for years

lesson.text: Delivery matters: eye contact round the room, the right volume for the back row, and clear pronunciation. Listen: a steady pace, with a pause before the key number.

Credit every source, on the slide or at the end, and check every number and chart is accurate. Practise with your media and time yourself. Keep any music under your voice quiet, and if the screen fails, carry on.

picture.title: Six in ten pieces
picture.notes: Pause, then say what it means.

lesson.text: Try it in the world: in Talk & Deal in the LIFE tab, pitch your bread cart to three investors, looking at each one as you speak. Next: use these skills in your grade 8 projects, such as the history documentary.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this a steady pace for a talk?
exercises.hint: Are the claps even, and slow enough to follow?
exercises.explain: True: the claps are even and unhurried, like a clear speaker.

exercises.prompt: Your talk is about how pupils travel to school. Which media helps most?
choices: a bar chart of how they travel
exercises.explain: A bar chart shows how many walk, cycle or ride, so it makes the point clearer; the others only distract.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this loud enough for the back of the room?
exercises.hint: Would someone far away hear it?
exercises.explain: False: it is very quiet. Speak up so that everyone in the room can hear.

exercises.prompt: Where should your full script go?
exercises.hint: The audience should listen to you, not read.
exercises.explain: In the speaker notes: the slides keep only key words, so the audience listens to you.

exercises.prompt: Match each point to the media that supports it.
items: what a coral reef looks like
exercises.hint: Ask what the audience needs to hear or see.
exercises.explain: A jet's loudness is heard: a recording. A place is shown on a map. Growth over time is a line graph. How a reef looks is a photo.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Where does the speaker pause?
exercises.explain: The claps come in two groups with a gap between: a pause after a main point, so listeners can think.

exercises.prompt: Sort the slide features: do they help the audience, or distract them?
exercises.hint: Could the audience take it in at a glance and keep listening?
exercises.explain: One idea, a clear chart and key words help; tiny text, spinning effects and clashing colours distract.

exercises.prompt: What is wrong with this slide?
choices: too much small text in clashing colours
exercises.hint: Could the audience read it at a glance?
exercises.explain: It is crammed with small text in clashing colours: the audience would read instead of listening.

exercises.prompt: Order the plan for a talk.
items: Sum up your findings in a sentence
Choose two or three salient points
exercises.hint: Know what you will say before you make the slides.
exercises.explain: Sum up the findings, choose the salient points, find their evidence, make simple slides, then practise with a timer.

exercises.prompt: Music under your voice should be quieter than you.
exercises.hint: What does the audience need to hear most?
exercises.explain: True: your words carry the point, so any music must stay quietly in the background.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a proper credit for a source, or not?
exercises.hint: A credit says who made it, so the audience could check it.
exercises.explain: The park service, the council survey and the mapping agency name who made them; the others give the audience nothing to check.

exercises.prompt: Listen: a tune like a voice, with music under it. What is wrong with the mix?
choices: the music is louder than the voice
exercises.hint: Which part do you hear most?
exercises.explain: The low chords drown the high tune: the music must be turned down so the voice carries the point.

exercises.hint: Grab attention first, then tell them where you are going.
exercises.explain: The hook grabs attention, the claim says what you will show, the plan says how, then the first point begins.

exercises.prompt: Halfway through your talk, the screen fails. Order what you do.
items: carry on with your next point
exercises.hint: Who knows what the chart showed? You do.
exercises.explain: Stay calm, tell the audience, describe the chart in words, then carry on: you know your evidence.

exercises.prompt: Listen: each clap is a word. Is this a good pace for the key point of a talk?
exercises.explain: False: it rushes with no pauses; slow down and pause before and after the key point.

exercises.prompt: The chart shows that 60 of 100 pieces of litter were plastic. Which sentence is accurate?
choices: Six in ten pieces were plastic.
Almost all the litter was plastic.
Plastic was a small part of it.
exercises.hint: Work out the share: 60 out of 100.
exercises.explain: 60 of 100 is 60%, or six in ten. “Almost all” overstates it, and “a small part” understates it.
